extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers of satirical/Renaissance comic literature; scholars and practitioners of humour in prose
extracted.subtask_description: Producing Rabelaisian-style satirical prose: mixing learned references, bodily grotesque humour, neologisms, hyperbole and digression to produce comic effect and social critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: plain_voice_vs_rhetorical_grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: I have made bold to choose to chirrup and warble my plain ditty, or, as they say, to whistle like a goose among the swans, rather than be thought deaf among so many pretty poets and eloquent orators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer a simple, plain, comic voice over ornate, high rhetorical manner when aiming for humour; present oneself as a playful 'clown' rather than imitating elevated poets. Example: explicitly choosing to 'chirrup and warble' instead of adopting crimson, alamode rhetorical flourishes. Anti-pattern: adopting lofty rhetorical grandiloquence when the comic aim is plainness and accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: embrace_the_clown_and_performative_role
rubrics_metrics.description: I am prouder of acting the clown, or any other under-part, among the many ingenious actors in that noble play, than of herding among those mutes ... who only serve to fill up the house and make up a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humour can come from willingly taking the low/performer role — self-deprecation, clowning and active comic performance are preferable to silent conformity. Being vivid and visible (acting the clown) is a positive comic stance. Anti-pattern: hiding behind pretence of solemnity or neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: parody_scholastic_obscurity
rubrics_metrics.description: the seer is ancient, the style laconic, the sentences dark like those of Scotus, though they treat of matters dark enough in themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Imitate dense, learned, or intentionally obscure scholastic phrasing to comedic effect — mock the style of authorities (Scotus, scholastics) to expose pomposity. Use erudite register ironically. Anti-pattern: actual incomprehensibility that loses the reader rather than amusing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: synonym_piling_and_long_enumeration
rubrics_metrics.description: Whole cartloads of books that seemed florid, flourishing, and flowery, gay, and gaudy as so many butterflies, but in the main were tiresome, dull, soporiferous, irksome, mischievous, crabbed, knotty, puzzling, and dark ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lists of synonyms, piling epithets, and extended enumerations to generate comic rhythm, excess, and mock-importance. Such catalogues create comedic accumulation and overstated emphasis. Example: long strings of adjectives. Anti-pattern: lists so long they obscure meaning without producing comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: grotesque_and_bodily_humour
rubrics_metrics.description: For they shall shell the shrub’s delicious fruit ... they farted like men, but stunk like devils ... For my part, I have no great stomach to fasting; for alas! it is as easy as pissing a bed ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ coarse, bodily, scatological imagery and frank references to digestion, farting, sex, excrement and other 'low' matters for earthy, grotesque humour. Bodily grotesquery is a deliberate device here. Anti-pattern: using such images gratuitously without satirical or comic purpose may alienate readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: satirical_encomium_and_exaggerated_praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Their works are all Parian marble, alabaster, porphyry, and royal cement; they treat of nothing but heroic deeds ... Their writings are all divine nectar, rich, racy, sparkling, delicate, and luscious wine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply extravagant, laudatory language ironically — overblown praise can serve as satire by exposing pretension. Use hyperbolic encomium to mock the objects being praised. Anti-pattern: genuine praise that lacks ironic distance when the goal is satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: mix_high_and_low_registers_for_contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: Since then ’tis not in my power to improve our architecture as much as they ... I am e’en resolved to do like Renault of Montauban: I’ll wait on the masons, set on the pot for the masons, cook for the stone-cutters;
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine classical, learned references with crude, everyday images and occupations to produce comedic contrast. Juxtaposing lofty allusion with kitchen or bodily detail heightens the absurdity. Anti-pattern: keeping register uniform which reduces the potential for comic dissonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: invented_taxonomy_and_neologisms
rubrics_metrics.description: He called the males clerg-hawks, monk-hawks, priest-hawks, abbot-hawks, bish-hawks, cardin-hawks, and one pope-hawk ... a fifth kind of cucullati newly stamped ... capus-hawks, more grum, vinegar-faced, brain-sick, froward, and loathsome ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coin playful compound words, invented species, and mock-classificatory terms (neologisms, portmanteaux) to parody institutional language and create comic world-building. Use whimsical taxonomy to satirize social categories. Anti-pattern: neologisms that confuse rather than amuse without context.

rubrics_metrics.name: digression_and_catalogic_aside
rubrics_metrics.description: Having taken this resolution, I thought it would not be amiss to move my Diogenical tub ... Whole cartloads of books ... In their stead beans in cod are started up ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use extended digressions, asides, and narrative detours to accumulate comic material, build voice, and create expectations that pay off later. Digressions can be used to lampoon authorities or to indulge in associative humour. Anti-pattern: digressions that never return or fail to contribute comic meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: hyperbole_and_absurd_exaggeration
rubrics_metrics.description: All manner of folly shall have an end, that being also numberless, according to Avicenna, maniae infinitae sunt species ... For, look here, though the sky were of brass, and the earth of iron, we should not want ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Push statements to absurd extremes and use grand-scale exaggeration to create comedy and to satirize claims of certainty or authority. Hyperbole helps demonstrate ridiculousness. Anti-pattern: hyperbole so extreme it becomes nonsensical rather than comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: mock_erudition_and_spoofing_pedantry
rubrics_metrics.description: I had a full account of all that Atteius Capito, Paulus, Marcellus, A. Gellius, Athenaeus, Suidas, Ammonius, and others had writ ... Beggarly scavengers that rake even the muddiest canals of antiquity for scraps and bits of Latin ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke lists of learned authorities, obscure citations, and footnote-like name-dropping to parody scholarly pretension; pairing that mock erudition with obvious silliness exposes pedantry. Anti-pattern: genuinely opaque references without humorous framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: onomatopoeia_sound-play_and_repetitive_jangle
rubrics_metrics.description: we heard a kind of a confused and often repeated noise ... not unlike the sound of great, middle-sized, and little bells rung all at once ... the nearer we came to the land the louder we heard that jangling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use onomatopoeic description, repeated sound-words, and ringing/jangling motifs to create comic atmosphere and sensory humour. Repetition of sound-words (ting-tang, jingle-jangle) can be a running gag. Anti-pattern: overuse without variation becoming merely noisy.
